cards.text: Moses, Israel's leader, is still preaching to all Israel (Deuteronomy 5:1). Today's topic is money, and Moses starts with a clock. At the end of every seven years, something big happens to debts.

cards.question: At the end of every seven years Israel must ___ debts.

cards.text: Every creditor cancels what he loaned to his neighbor and collects nothing from his brother. Picture opening your credit card bill and the whole thing just says NEVER MIND.

cards.question: Why does the lender stop collecting from his neighbor?

answers.text: The LORD's time of release has been proclaimed
The neighbor has already paid it back twice
The elders at the city gate have voided it

cards.question: The year of release also wipes out what a foreigner owes an Israelite.

cards.text: Then Moses says there will be no poor among them, because the LORD will surely bless them in the land He's giving them. Read that one twice, friend. No poor among you. WHAT?

cards.question: Moses says the LORD's blessing in the land, with no poor among them, comes with a condition: Israel obeys the LORD and carefully follows His commands.
When the LORD blesses them as He promised, Israel will ___ to many nations but borrow from none, and ___ over many nations but be ruled by none.

cards.text: But if there's a poor man among their brothers, Moses says don't harden your heart or shut your hand. No going quiet in the group chat the second somebody types 'Hey, so, um…'

cards.question: Instead of shutting his hand, what is an Israelite to do for his poor brother?

answers.text: Open his hand and loan what he needs
Point him to a richer man in town
Hire him to work for one season

cards.text: Then Moses calls out a wicked thought: the seventh year, the year of release, is near. That man is looking at his brother, but he's thinking about the CALENDAR.

cards.question: What does Moses warn that wicked thought about the year of release will lead to?
If that poor brother cries out to the LORD against him, Moses says the man who gave nothing will be guilty of sin.

cards.text: So give generously, Moses says, and don't let your heart be grieved when you do. No handing it over with the face I make when I give away the LAST chocolate chip cookie.

cards.question: Because of that generous giving, the LORD will ___ them in all their work.

cards.text: Moses is honest about it: there will never cease to be poor in the land. That's exactly why he's giving this command.

cards.question: Who does Moses command Israel to open wide their hand to?

answers.text: Their brother and the poor and needy
Only the Levites within their gates
Only the elders of their own city

cards.text: Now Moses moves from loans to servants. Say a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, is sold to you and serves you six years.

cards.question: In the seventh year, the master must ___ the Hebrew servant who served him six years.

cards.text: And when he goes, don't send him away empty-handed. Six years of work and you walk out with a handshake and a box of your own stuff? NOT HERE.

cards.question: The master sends his servant off with plenty from his flock, his threshing floor and his winepress. How much does he give?

answers.text: As the LORD has blessed him
One tenth of that year's harvest

cards.question: What does Moses tell Israel to remember as the reason for this command?

answers.text: They were slaves in Egypt and the LORD redeemed them
Freed servants will speak well of their old masters
The nations around them are watching how they live

cards.text: But what if the servant says, 'I do not want to leave you,' because he loves you and your household and he's well off with you? Friend, I spent years in a drawer waiting for that thing to open, and this man gets the door WIDE open and says nah, I'm good.

cards.question: When the servant chooses to stay, what does the master do with an awl?

answers.text: Pierce his ear into the door
Carve his name into the gate
Mark the year on the doorpost

cards.question: A servant who stays this way serves for life, and a maidservant is treated the same way.

cards.text: Moses tells them not to regard it as a hardship to set a servant free. And he's got the math to back it up.

cards.question: The servant's six years of service were worth ___ the wages of a hired hand.

cards.text: Last topic: every firstborn male from their herds and flocks is set apart to the LORD their God.

cards.question: A firstborn ox that's set apart to the LORD can still be put to work.
Each year, where does the household eat the firstborn male animal set apart to the LORD?

answers.text: Before the LORD at the place He chooses
Down in the land of Goshen in Egypt
Beside the Jordan River near Jericho

cards.text: But some firstborn come out with a defect, or lame, or blind, or with some other serious flaw. Kind of like my old stamps back when my edges were worn down.

cards.question: A firstborn animal with a serious flaw can still be sacrificed to the LORD.

cards.text: Those flawed ones get eaten at home, within their gates, the way they'd eat a gazelle or a deer. Not for the altar. For the house.

cards.question: Who may eat a flawed firstborn animal at home?

answers.text: Both the unclean and the clean
Only the priests and the Levites
Only the head of the household

cards.question: When they eat a flawed firstborn animal at home, they must not eat the ___ but pour it on the ground like water.

cards.text: And that's where we'll set this batch down for now. Keep that apron on, friend, because Moses is NOT done preaching.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: 'Then Moses says…', 'Read that one twice, friend.', 'No poor among you.' and 'WHAT?' Story cards after the opening card can have at most two.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The statement turns Deuteronomy 15:9 into a condition: 'If that poor brother cries out… the man who gave nothing will be guilty of sin.' The text says 'He will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.' It never makes the guilt depend on the cry, so the card adds an 'if' and a link the text doesn't state.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Both wrong answers start with 'Only' ('Only the Levites…', 'Only the elders…'), but the right answer doesn't. The right answer is also the only one that fits a stop that has been about the poor brother the whole time. It stands out from the other two.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'And when he goes…', 'Six years of work…?' and 'NOT HERE.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Card 5 just told the baker the LORD redeemed Israel from slavery in Egypt. After that, 'Down in the land of Goshen in Egypt' isn't a believable place to eat an offering each year. The right answer also stands out, because it repeats 'the LORD' from the question.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'Those flawed ones…', 'Not for the altar.' and 'For the house.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Deuteronomy 15:22 says 'Eat it within your gates,' which means in their towns. The card calls this 'at home' and 'For the house,' and cards 17 and 18 repeat 'at home.' The text doesn't call it that.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Both wrong answers start with 'Only' ('Only the priests…', 'Only the head…'), but the right answer doesn't. Card 16 also just compared the meat to a gazelle or a deer, so the right answer is the only one that doesn't sound restricted. It stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: Deuteronomy 15:19-23 gives rules for firstborn animal offerings. 'Rules for offerings and feasts' is on the long-stretch list, but here the rules get four story cards and four choice cards (cards 11-18). Moses is giving a speech, though, and speeches are listed as not a long stretch. The servant law in 15:12-18 has the same tension: the Exodus 21-23 example treats servant laws as a long stretch of everyday rules.
findings.question: In a Sermons passage where the sermon itself is made of laws, like Moses' speeches in Deuteronomy, do stretches of offering rules or everyday rules count as long stretches (one summary story card, no choice cards)? Or does the 'speeches' exemption cover the whole passage?
